## Map fields to channels

Each channel maps to an **encoding object** `{ field, ... }` (or a bare
string shorthand, expanded to `{ field: "<string>" }`):

```json
"encodings": {
  "x": { "field": "weight" },
  "y": "mpg",
  "color": { "field": "origin" }
}
```

**Encoding object fields** (all optional except `field`):

| Field | Values | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `field` | column name | Bind the channel to a data column |
| `type` | `quantitative`, `nominal`, `ordinal`, `temporal` | Override the inferred encoding type (rarely needed) |
| `aggregate` | `count`, `sum`, `average`, `mean` | Force an aggregation on a measure channel. A heatmap that gets several rows per cell aggregates its colour on its own (sum for additive types such as `Quantity` or `Profit`, average otherwise) and warns; set `aggregate` to choose |
| `sortOrder` | `ascending`, `descending` | Sort direction; in Vega-Lite, direction alone preserves/reverses the semantic sequence |
| `sortBy` | mapped `"x"`, `"y"`, `"color"`; Vega-Lite also accepts a data field or JSON-array string | Explicit category ordering; see the Vega-Lite contract below |
| `scheme` | Vega scheme name (e.g. `viridis`, `redblue`), or a list of stops low end first (`["#c0392b", "#f2f2f2", "#2e75b6"]`) | Color scheme for the `color` channel; wins over the theme's ramp |
| `reverse` | `true` / `false` | `color` only: run the color scale the other way round |
| `mid` | number | `color` only: where a diverging scale pivots, for this chart (the field's `divergingMidpoint`) |
| `domain` | `[low, high]` | `color` only: the measure extent the ramp spans, in place of the data's |
| `bins` | integer ≥ 2, or `0` | `color` only: quantize a continuous measure into that many steps; `0` keeps the ramp continuous |
| `colors` | `{ value: color }` | `color` only: colors bound to category values, for this chart (the field's `colors`) |
| `title` | a string, or `null` | The name the channel's axis or key prints in place of the field's; `null` prints none |

You usually don't need `type`, `aggregate`, or `sortOrder` — they're
inferred from the semantic type. Set them only with specific intent.

**Vega-Lite sorting.** Omit sorting for canonical Month/Day/Quarter order.
`sortOrder` alone follows that semantic sequence (descending reverses it),
not alphabetical month names. Without a semantic sequence, direction alone
uses the field's native value order.

- `sortBy: "month_number"` sorts by that existing data field, ascending by
  default. Multiple rows per category use the minimum sort-field value.
- `sortBy: "y"` sorts by the mapped channel; cross-channel sorts default to
  descending, while self-channel sorts default to ascending. `x`, `y`, and
  `color` are reserved channel names and must be mapped.
- `sortBy: "[\"Mar\",\"Jan\",\"Feb\"]"` supplies an explicit category order;
  `sortOrder: "descending"` reverses it. Use a JSON-array **string**, not an array
  or a Vega-Lite sort object. Members must be strings, numbers, or booleans.
- For explicit lexical ordering of month labels, sort by the category field
  itself: `{ "field": "month", "sortBy": "month", "sortOrder": "ascending" }`.

Unknown fields, unmapped channels, invalid directions, and malformed sort
arrays are errors, not fallback orders. Raw field-name sorting is currently
supported by the Vega-Lite backend; for other backends use their supported
channel-sort controls. Validate inputs against the selected backend.

**Multi-series (wide → long).** To plot several measure columns as series,
pass an **array** on `x` or `y` (only those two channels). The library
folds them into long form and synthesizes a series/legend field:

```json
"encodings": { "x": { "field": "month" }, "y": ["sales", "profit"] }
```

All array fields must be quantitative, and you cannot also bind `color`
when using the array form (the fold owns the color/legend). This is the
**only** built-in reshape — there is no `transforms`/`fold` property. For any
other shape (long↔wide, an aggregate the encodings can't express, a derived
column, a pivot, a join), reshape the data first with a host tool — pandas/polars,
Arquero/`Array.map`/SQL, or a data/MCP tool — and pass the result as
`data.values`. If you have no way to transform, surface the gap to the developer
rather than inventing a transform property that does not exist.

## Semantic types

**This matters most.** Semantic types drive all downstream
decisions — formatting, zero baseline, color scheme, scale direction, and
more. Pick the most specific type for each field. Full registered set:

| Family | Semantic types |
|---|---|
| Temporal (point) | `DateTime`, `Date`, `Time`, `Timestamp` |
| Temporal (granule) | `Year`, `Quarter`, `Month`, `Week`, `Day`, `Hour`, `YearMonth`, `YearQuarter`, `YearWeek`, `Decade` |
| Temporal (span) | `Duration` |
| Measure (amount) | `Amount`, `Price`, `Quantity`, `Count` |
| Measure (generic) | `Number` — a measure whose values should not be added up (or whose additivity is unknown); use `Count`, `Amount`, `Quantity` or `Profit` for totals |
| Measure (proportion) | `Percentage` |
| Measure (signed/diverging) | `Profit`, `PercentageChange`, `Sentiment`, `Correlation` |
| Measure (physical) | `Temperature` |
| Discrete / rank | `Rank`, `Score`, `ID` |
| Geographic (coord) | `Latitude`, `Longitude` |
| Geographic (place) | `Country`, `State`, `City`, `Region`, `Address`, `ZipCode` |
| Categorical | `Category`, `Name`, `Status`, `Boolean`, `Direction`, `Range` |
| Fallback | `Unknown` |

A temporal type also tells Flint how to read the values: a `YearMonth` accepts `202501`, `2025-01`, `2025/1`, `01/2025`, `2025M01`, `Jan 2025`, `2025-Jul`, `July-2025` or `Jul '25`; a `Date` accepts `20250115`, `2025/01/15`, `Jan 15, 2025` or `15-Jan-2025`. Pass the values as they are; an untyped field is never reinterpreted.

What choosing well gets you (automatically):

- `Price` / `Amount` → currency formatting, zero baseline, sequential color
- `Temperature` → diverging color scheme, no forced zero baseline
- `Correlation` → fixed `[-1, 1]` diverging domain
- `Rank` → reversed axis (1 on top), discrete color
- `Date` / `DateTime` → temporal axis with auto-granularity formatting
- `Percentage` → percent formatting, 0–100 domain awareness

If you don't know, use `Quantity` for numbers that add up to a total and
`Number` for ones that don't, `Category` for strings,
`Date`/`DateTime` for date-shaped values. Do **not** invent type names.

### Saying more than the type name

A field's entry can be an object instead of a string when the type alone
understates what you know:

```json
"semantic_types": {
  "anomaly": { "semanticType": "Quantity", "unit": "°C", "divergingMidpoint": 0 },
  "rating":  { "semanticType": "Score", "intrinsicDomain": [1, 5] }
}
```

- `unit` — an optional assertion that authorizes Flint to display a unit. Add
  it only when the data or surrounding context establishes the measurement
  and seeing it materially changes how a reader interprets the number. A type
  such as `Duration`, a field name such as `life_expectancy`, or values that
  merely look plausible are not enough evidence by themselves.
  - Prefer canonical codes: `"USD"`, `"°C"`, `"kg"`, `"km/h"`, `"min"`.
  - Conventional compact units are normalized and may appear beside values
    (`USD` → `$`, `hours` → `hr`).
  - Lexical units such as `"years"` are stated once beside the field name as
    `field (years)`, not repeated after every value.
  - Do not put explanatory phrases in `unit`. Put qualifications such as
    `"per working-age resident"` or `"constant 2024 prices"` in the subtitle.
  - Omit `unit` when its meaning, scale, or denominator is uncertain. Flint
    does not infer a visible unit from the semantic type or field name.
- `intrinsicDomain` — the field's own bounds, for bounded scales only: `[1, 5]`
  for a five-star rating, `[0, 100]` for a percentage score. Not for
  open-ended measures.
- `percentScale` — `"fraction"` or `"percent"`: how a `Percentage` or
  `PercentageChange` field is stored (0.45 or 45 for 45%). Set it when you know;
  otherwise Flint guesses from the values, which misreads fractions mostly past
  1 (growth of 2.4 meaning 240%).
- `divergingMidpoint` — where the middle colour of a diverging scale sits.
  Set it if you can tell what the reader is comparing against; leave it out if
  you can't.
- `divergingNeutral` — for a colour stepped into classes, how far either side
  of the midpoint still reads as neither side: `0.1` makes correlations within
  ±0.1 one neutral class; `false` makes the midpoint a break, so a small gain
  never looks like a small loss. Leave it out and the type decides
  (`Correlation`, `Sentiment`: a neutral class; `Profit`, `PercentageChange`:
  a break).
- `sortOrder` — the order the categories should appear in, when the order in
  the data is not the one you want and it isn't alphabetical either:
  `["Low", "Medium", "High"]`. For a handful of categories, not a long list.
- `colors` — colours that belong to particular values, when the data has a
  convention the reader expects: `{ "DFL": "#0793AB", "Republican": "#A1000F" }`.
  Matched on the value (case-insensitive); values left out take the palette,
  which then skips these colours. Only for real conventions (parties, brands,
  asset classes), not to restyle a chart — the theme owns the palette.
- `polarity` — `"higher-is-better"` or `"lower-is-better"`: which end of a
  diverging colour is the alarming one. Signed measures (`Profit`,
  `PercentageChange`) read as higher-is-better on their own; set
  `"lower-is-better"` for costs, errors, churn or delays, so their highs, not
  their lows, take the warm end, under any theme.

## Write a headline

Set `chart_spec.title` to the finding, in a sentence, and `chart_spec.subtitle`
to the reading of it — what is measured, of whom, when, in what units:

```
title:    "A pyramid that is no longer a pyramid"
subtitle: "United States population by age and sex, 2020, millions"
```

Add `chart_spec.label` only when the chart sits in a numbered sequence or
under a section name: `label: "Figure 2"`. It is drawn above the headline in
the theme's kicker style.

`chart_spec.source` is optional. Add it only when the user names the source or
asks for a source line, or the data itself states where it comes from:
`source: "UN World Population Prospects 2024"` (or `{ text, href }` to link
it). Never invent or guess one. The theme decides how it reads ("Source:",
side, rule, credit); a chart without one draws no footer.

`chart_spec.chrome` is the house decoration the theme draws around the chart:
header rules, tabs, wordmarks, logos, the footer rule and the house credit. It is
not the chart's own title, label or source. The theme draws it by default; leave
`chrome` out unless the user asks to drop it: `chrome: false`
drops all of it; `chrome: { logos: false }` (or `header`, `footer: false`) drops
one part. Without logos a credit keeps its words.

`Jan`, `Cairo`, `Chrome` name their own kind; `26`, `5,300`, `0.42` do not, and
the headline is where they get named. Leave it out only where the chart is not
read on its own — a sparkline in a cell, a tile under its own caption. Nothing
breaks: with no headline to lean on, the compiler keeps the axis titles instead.

## Write the spec

One `ChartAssemblyInput`, with the data bound as in "How data gets bound" and
a headline as in "Write a headline":

```json
{
  "data": { "url": "sales.csv" },
  "semantic_types": { "month": "YearMonth", "revenue": "Amount", "region": "Region" },
  "chart_spec": {
    "chartType": "Line Chart",
    "title": "Europe climbed every month after the April dip",
    "subtitle": "Revenue by region, $m",
    "encodings": { "x": { "field": "month" }, "y": { "field": "revenue" }, "color": { "field": "region" } }
  }
}
```

The full shape:

```ts
interface ChartAssemblyInput {
  // Bound by the HOST or by you, as in "How data gets bound".
  data: { values: any[] } | { url: string };
  semantic_types?: Record<string, string | SemanticAnnotation>;  // field → type ( ← you write this)
  chart_spec: {                               //                        ← you write this
    chartType: string;                        // e.g. "Scatter Plot"
    title?: string;                           // the headline — write one
    subtitle?: string;                        // what is measured, of whom, when, in what units
    label?: string;                           // a figure number or kicker, above the headline
    source?: string | { text: string; href?: string }; // only when known; never invented
    chrome?: false | { header?: false; footer?: false; logos?: false }; // drop the house's decoration
    encodings: Record<string, EncodingValue>; // channel → { field, ... } (or array)
    baseSize?: { width: number; height: number };    // target layout size, default 400×320
    canvasSize?: { width: number; height: number };  // optional hard ceiling on stretch
    chartProperties?: Record<string, any>;    // per-chart tuning (optional)
  };
  options?: Record<string, any>;              // global layout options (rarely needed)
  field_display_names?: Record<string, string>; // field → readable axis/legend title
  theme_spec?: string | { extends: string; [key: string]: any }; // preset or preset override (Vega-Lite, Plotly)
  interaction_spec?: { interactions: { type: string; id?: string; options?: Record<string, any> }[] }; // behaviour (interaction skill)
  updates?: { id: string; ops: any[] }[];     // the agent's marks on the chart (interaction skill)
}
```

Set `chartProperties` only when the user asks for that behaviour; defaults
are sensible. Global layout `options` are rarely needed.

A mounted chart already shows a tooltip and lets a legend click dim a group.
Add more only for a reason:

- `interaction_spec` (behaviour): the user asks for a gesture or describes

  data has more detail than the chart can show at its size.
- `updates` (marks the agent leaves: a note, emphasis, a shaded range, a
  reference line): the user asks for marks on the chart, asks about a chart
  on screen, or asks a concrete question the chart can point at lightly.

# flint-chart: interactions and updates on a chart

Two things go beside a chart input, and both are optional:

- `interaction_spec`: behaviour, what the reader can do. `{ "interactions": [ { "type": <preset>, "options"?: { … } } ] }`.
- `updates`: state, marks the agent leaves on the chart (notes, emphasis, a
  shaded range, a reference line). A list of `{ "id", "ops": [ … ] }` layers.

A gesture's handler and an agent write the same layers, so when the request
is for something the reader can do themselves, give them the gesture; when it
is a point the agent makes, write the update. The chart itself is the
`flint-chart-author` skill. Everything here runs on the Vega-Lite backend; a
static render and the other backends ignore both. Code (mounting, `onChange`,
linking charts in an app, a gesture no preset gives) is the `flint-app-author`
skill; on an MCP board, charts connect through `link_spec` (the
`flint-board-author` skill).

Use only the names in this skill and in `list_interaction_presets`. When the
request asks for a behaviour no preset gives, say which preset comes closest
and what it leaves out.

## Add interactions

### When

A mounted chart already shows each mark's values in a tooltip, and a click on
a legend item dims the other groups. Add behaviour only for a reason:

1. **The user asks for it**, by naming a gesture ("brush a period", "zoom",
   "toggle the legend") or by describing what the chart should do ("click a
   line so it stands out", "slide along the years", "let me pick the year").
   "Make it interactive" is an ask with nothing named: one or two presets
   that fit the chart.
2. **The chart works with other charts** on a board: behaviour is what
   connects the views.
3. **The data needs it to be read**: more detail than the chart can show at
   its size (a long dense series, a crowded cluster, a map) that the reader
   will want to see closer. Shape the chart first (an aggregate, a scale, a
   filter); behaviour is a way to move closer (`navigate`, `brush-zoom`). Many
   series is not this reason: fewer series is a shaping choice, and picking
   them apart waits for the user to ask.

Otherwise add nothing. A question about the data is answered by the chart and
the reply, and a chart shown in a live view has asked for nothing.

### Pick presets

Take the preset whose gesture the user named, or whose purpose meets what
they described, one per job and as few jobs as the reason holds: one or two
entries for most charts, none added to round out a set.
`list_interaction_presets` with `chartType` lists the presets the type
supports, what each needs, its reset and every option.

| Preset | Gesture | What it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Single one thing out** | | |
| `click-highlight` | Clicks a mark, a legend item, or an axis label; it stays emphasised and the rest mute. Shift-click adds. | Keeps one mark, series, or category in focus against the rest while the reader looks at it; in an app, the selection the app reads. |
| `click-group-focus` | Clicks a mark; every mark in its group stays emphasised. `groupBy` names the group field. | Follows one group (a country's line, a species' points) across the chart from any of its marks. |
| `hover-group-focus` | Hovers a mark; its group stands out until the pointer leaves. `groupBy` names the group field; `emphasis` is `"auto"` (a line widens and the rest stay as drawn; points, bars, and slices dim the rest), `"highlight"`, or `"spotlight"`. | Picks one group out of many overlapping ones at a glance, without a click. |
| `axis-highlight` | Clicks (or with `event: "hover"`, hovers) a discrete axis label; that category's marks emphasise. | Picks a whole row or column, a category or a month, through its axis label. |
| **Read values** | | |
| `inspect` | Moves over the plot; a guide follows the pointer and the nearest mark on the chosen axes reads out. `mode` picks the axes and a comparison (`"x>"` reads every mark past the pointer). | Reads exact positions on guides: a crosshair on one or both axes, or every mark past a threshold. One mark's values are already in the tooltip. |
| `inspect-index` | Moves along the index axis; every series reads out at that position on one guide, each value labelled in its series colour and the position named at the axis. `show: "single"` reads one series and switches it through the legend; `seriesBy` names the series field when the chart draws one series at a time; `displayValue: false` keeps the guides and drops the labels. | Reads several series at the same position side by side, on one guide. With one series it repeats the tooltip. |
| **Focus a region** | | |
| `select` | Drags a rectangle; the marks inside emphasise. `mode: "stateful"` keeps the rectangle on screen to move and resize. | Picks out the marks in an area of a two-dimensional spread, to see which they are. |
| `lasso-select` | Draws a freehand region; the marks inside emphasise. | Picks out an irregular cluster that a rectangle would not fit. |
| `brush-x`, `brush-y` | Drags an interval along one axis; the marks in it emphasise. `mode: "stateful"` keeps the interval on screen to move and resize. On a polar chart the x brush is a sector. | Marks a period or a value range, to see what falls in it. |
| `brush-angle` | Drags an angular sector on a pie, donut, rose, or radar; the slices in it emphasise. | Takes adjacent slices of a part-to-whole chart together. |
| `linked-brush` | Drags a region; the groups inside emphasise in every chart that mounts the same preset. `groupBy` names the shared field; `mode: 'stateful'` keeps the rectangle on screen to move or resize. | Connects charts: groups picked in one show in every chart that shares the field. |
| **Move the view** | | |
| `navigate` | Drags to pan; wheels or pinches to zoom a continuous axis. `axes` limits it; `pan: false` leaves the plot drag free. On a map it moves the projection; on a globe (a world Choropleth with `projection: "orthographic"`) a drag turns the sphere and the zoom stays centred. On a map, `geometry.domain.focus` names the region at the centre. | Moves through a chart that holds more detail than fits at its size: a long series, a dense cluster, a map. |
| `brush-zoom` | Drags a rectangle; the chart flies into it. | Jumps into one stretch or box of a dense chart, and back out. |

- `drag-reorder` needs a discrete axis in the bound encodings.
- `inspect-index` needs an index axis, which it finds itself: the temporal
  axis, else the discrete axis beside a measure, else x. A horizontal bar
  chart reads along y with no option; `axis` overrides the choice. `seriesBy`
  names the series field when the chart draws one series at a time.
- `click-group-focus`, `hover-group-focus`, and `linked-brush` need `groupBy`,
  a bound field.

### Write and validate

Every entry is `{ "type": <preset>, "id"?: <string>, "options"?: { ... } }`:
options nest under `options` (`reset` is one of them, set only to free a
trigger), and `id` sits on the entry, needed only when one preset appears
twice.

```json
{
  "interactions": [
    { "type": "click-highlight", "options": { "targets": ["mark"] } },
    { "type": "legend-toggle" }
  ]
}
```

`show` checks it as it draws (`validate_chart` without a card).
An unknown `type`, an option beside `type`, an `id` inside `options` or a
missing required option is an error. A dropped or yielded entry is a warning
that names the entry and what it needed:

```
Interaction "legend-toggle" requires a discrete legend; Bar Chart has none. The interaction was dropped.
```

Fix or drop what it warns about.

## Update the chart

A chart opens clean. `updates` add the agent's own marks to it only for one
of these reasons; without one, what the agent wants to say goes in its reply.

1. **The user asks for marks on the chart.** They name one ("label the peak",
   "highlight Japan", "a line at $3", "shade the recession"), or describe a
   chart that has to tell its point on its own ("for a slide").
2. **The user asks about a chart already on screen.** The answer points at
   the chart: emphasise the rows, note the value, frame the range.
3. **A requested interaction needs a starting state.** "Look at one year,
   then slide along" opens on that year with `set-viewport`.
4. **A concrete question, pointed at lightly**, as below.

### Muted annotations

A question about particular values (a peak, a value at a date, a difference,
a crossing, a threshold, which items pass one) may point at its answer
without being asked. An overview question ("how did it move", "is there a
relationship") gets none.

- **The title says it; the annotation points.** The answer is in the title
  (and the reply). On the chart, only what directly answers the question: one
  mark, two for a difference or a crossing, one span, or one small set.
- **A label names what it points at.** A few words that still mean something
  on their own: the value and what identifies it ("$5.01 · Jun 13, 2022",
  "China 26, Russia 23"). Not a bare tag ("Peak", "Max"), not a sentence, not
  a repeat of the title or of a value label the chart already prints.
- **Room decides the form, not the chart type.** Where there is open space
  beside the answer, a short label. Where marks fill the space round it (a
  full grid of cells, a dense cluster, a bar that already prints its value),
  the highlight alone: `annotate-text` with `text: ""` draws the ring or
  outline and no caption. Many answers (more than three or four) get emphasis
  with no labels, and the list goes in the reply.
- **Light forms.** A mark: `annotate-text` with the default `highlight:
  'light'`, or `'strong'` for an outline. A span or band: one
  `annotate-region` under the marks, low opacity, a caption only when the
  title does not give the range and the plot has room above it. A small set:
  `set-style` with `state: 'emphasized'`, `emphasis: 'light'`, or an outline
  per member. A clear cluster: one `annotate-enclosure`, no caption when the
  legend names it. A value the question names: a plain `set-overlay` rule.
- **The answer is in view.** A pointer on a mark the reader cannot see is
  nothing. On a chart that scrolls or opens zoomed (a long heatmap, a wide
  calendar), narrow the data to the stretch that holds the answer, or open
  the viewport on it.
- **Not muted:** notes that tell a story, several shaded episodes, context the
  question did not ask about, `strong` or `exclusive` emphasis. Those need an
  ask (reason 1).

Text and paint come from the theme: notes take its annotation type, rings,
outlines and enclosures its `interaction.highlight`. Set them per update
(`value.style`, `value.highlightStyle`) only when the user asks.

### The state

After every build and every committed gesture, the MCP chart view sends the
agent the card's state in field terms: the chart after the reader's panel
edits, each op of your updates as applied (✓) or not and why (✗), what the
reader selected, hid or filtered, and the viewport. Read it before writing,
so an update does not undo what the reader set. The rows you were given are
the source of every value; nothing is computed that the chart cannot verify.

### Ops

| Op | It is for | Effect | Shape | Needs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `set-style` | The marks the chart already draws: emphasize some, fade some, hide some, recolour some. A highlight is this op with `state: 'emphasized'`. | Emphasize the targets and recede the rest; recolour; fade; hide. `emphasis` sets how far the rest recede: `'light'` (default; they stay readable), `'strong'`, `'exclusive'` (only the targets read). | `{ op, targets: UpdateTarget[], value: StyleSpec }` | marks |
| `annotate-text` | One mark, a stretch of a line or area, a leg of a map route (`visual: { kind: 'path' }` on the row it leaves from), a slice or a region that should carry a note. | Set a caption beside it: plain words haloed in the page, a leader only where needed, never a card; `null` clears it. `highlight` marks what it names: `'none'`, `'light'` (default), `'strong'`, `'exclusive'` (the rest recede, so no separate `set-style` emphasis is needed). The caption takes the theme's annotation type (else the axis labels' face a size up); `style` sets one note's `fontSize`, `fontWeight` or `color`; `highlightStyle: { color, width }` its ring or outline, over the theme's `interaction.highlight`. `text: ""` draws the highlight alone (an outline or ring, no caption); with `text` omitted the chart words the note itself. For a boxed callout use `set-overlay` or `set-freeform-overlay`. `set-annotation` is its deprecated name; do not write it. | `{ op, target: UpdateTarget, value: { text, anchor?: 'segment' \| 'point', highlight?, style?: { fontSize?, fontWeight?, color? }, highlightStyle?: { color?, width? } } \| null }` | one resolved element |
| `annotate-region` | A stretch of the plot: a period, a band of values, a box, a run of categories. | Shade it, with an optional caption set on it; `null` clears it. | `{ op, name, value: { x?: [lo, hi] \| categories, y?: [lo, hi] \| categories, text?, color?, opacity?, layer?: 'under' \| 'over', placement?: 'top' \| 'bottom' \| 'left' \| 'right' \| 'center' \| 'above' \| 'below' } \| null }`; on a map `longitude: [west, east], latitude: [south, north]` in place of x and y | x or y scales, or a map (not a pie or radar) |
| `annotate-enclosure` | A group of marks that belong together: a cluster, a run of bars, a block of cells. | Outline each target group; one optional caption shared by them, with leaders to two or three outlines; `null` clears it. | `{ op, name, value: { targets: UpdateTarget[], text?, shape?: 'hull' \| 'rect' \| 'ellipse' \| 'circle', connect?: 'auto' \| 'all' \| 'none', color?, width? } \| null }` | marks |
| `set-viewport` | The range or region the chart should frame. | Frame a continuous domain. | `{ op, axes: 'x' \| 'y' \| 'xy', value: { x?: [lo, hi], y?: [lo, hi] } }`; on a multi-level map `value: { region: { key } }` | `navigate` or `brush-zoom` mounted on that axis |
| `set-order` | The order of the categories on a discrete axis. | Reorder the axis; list every category in the order wanted. | `{ op, scope: 'category', field, values: unknown[] }` | `drag-reorder` mounted on that axis |
| `set-overlay` | Marks the chart does not draw: a reference line, a threshold band, a forecast, a sketch of rows. | Draw new rows through the plot's own scales. | `{ op, name, value: { mark, data: { values }, encodings: { x?, y?, x2?, y2?, order?, color?, text? }, role, interactive?, projectable?, style? } \| null }`; on a map `longitude`, `latitude` (and `longitude2`, `latitude2` for a rule or rect) in place of x and y | x and y scales, or a map |
| `set-freeform-overlay` | A custom shape with no data behind it. | Draw SVG, or a clone of marks, over the plot. | `{ op, name, value: { coordinateSpace: 'plot' \| 'renderer', body: [{ type: 'svg', content } \| { type: 'clone', targets, transform?, opacity? }] } \| null }` | — |
| `set-data` | The rows the chart draws, for playback or a swap. | Replace every row; the rows carry every encoded field. | `{ op, source: 'main', value: { rows } }` | inline data |

`StyleSpec` is `{ state?, emphasis?, opacity?, visible?, fill?, stroke?,
strokeWidth?, mutedOpacity? }`. Two states matter from outside: `emphasized`
keeps the targets at full ink and recedes every other mark by `emphasis`
(`'light'` by default, `'strong'`, `'exclusive'`; `mutedOpacity` sets the level
outright); `normal` with `targets: []` clears the layer. `opacity` on the
targets fades a subset and leaves the rest alone; `opacity: 0` hides marks and
keeps the axes, where `visible: false` removes the rows and shrinks the scales.

Overlay marks are `line`, `point`, `rule`, `rect`, `text`. `encodings` name
fields of the overlay's own rows, projected through the chart's x, y, and
colour scales. `style` takes `stroke`, `strokeWidth`, `strokeDash` (lengths, or
`'dash'` / `'dot'`), `fill`,
`fillOpacity`, `opacity`, `pointRadius`, `fontSize`, `fontWeight`, `fontStyle` (`italic`), `textAlign`
(`start`, `middle`, `end`), `dx`, `dy`. A `line` takes its stroke and a `text`
its fill from the `color` encoding; a `point` takes `style.fill`. A `text` sits on
the data, so it draws a halo in the chart's background; `stroke` sets another
colour, `strokeWidth` its width, and `stroke: 'none'` drops it, as a faint
watermark wants.

Two ops need a preset the chart mounts: `set-viewport` needs `navigate` or
`brush-zoom` on that axis, `set-order` needs `drag-reorder`. The host says
which are mounted, or the state shows `viewport` and `categoryOrder`. On a
chart that mounts neither, say so and offer an emphasis; `set-data` replaces
what the chart shows and is not a frame. Legend values belong to
`legend-toggle`: no update hides or restores one, and a series fades with
`opacity` instead.

### Targets and values

A target is one of three forms:

```ts
{ select: { key: { Country: 'Japan' } } }                 // marks with these values
{ select: { where: { Region: { in: ['Asia', 'Europe'] }, Month: { range: ['2025-03', '2025-06'] } } } }  // a set of marks
{ visual: { kind: 'mark', role: 'mark' }, elements }      // elements from an event or the state
```

- A `where` describes a set, in the words filters use: each field `in` a list
  or within a `range` (ends included; `null` leaves an end open), and every
  field must hold. Use it for a period, a band of values, or several categories
  at once, where a key would need one target per row. `set-style` and an
  enclosure's targets take a `where`; a note or an order names one mark, so it
  takes a key.
- Use the annotation ops to put a message on the chart: a note
  (`annotate-text`) on a mark, a shaded region (`annotate-region`) over a
  stretch of the plot (two bounds on a continuous axis, `null` for the plot's
  end, or adjacent categories on a banded one), or an outline
  (`annotate-enclosure`) round a group of marks, each with optional text.
  Leave colour, shape and placement to the chart unless the request names
  them. A note marks its own target through `highlight`; do not pair it with
  a `set-style` emphasis to make the mark stand out. A stretch of a line or
  area that spans a period is a region, not a note on one segment.

- A selector key names fields the chart encodes (`x`, `y`, `color`, `detail`,
  `size`, …) and matches rows by equality, so `'2007'` and `2007` differ. One
  key may cover many marks (`{ Continent: 'Africa' }` takes every African
  mark); several fields narrow it; an annotation's key covers one. On a line
  or area chart, a key on the series field covers the whole line and a key on
  the x field covers the segment that starts at that row, so a run of segments
  is one target per row. The last row of a line starts no segment; its key
  takes the segment that ends there. A note on an x key marks the segment, for
  a change from one row to the next ("2019 → 2020: +4%"); `anchor: "point"`
  marks the row's own point, for its value ("Dec 2022: $0.87B"). A note on
  the last row is always at its point.
- Annotation text says what the chart does not ("Promotion launched", "Lowest
  in Q3"), not a value or label it already prints (`note_repeats_chart`). The
  title states the finding; a note puts its specifics on the mark, and names

name: flint-theme-author
description: "Use when: creating, translating, refining, reviewing, or validating a custom Flint ThemeSpec from brand guidelines, websites, slide decks, publication references, design tokens, or an existing visual identity. Produce a reusable ThemeSpec JSON object for Flint Theme Lab without inventing fields or changing chart semantics."
---

# Flint ThemeSpec authoring

Create a reusable visual system for Flint charts. Translate the user's reference
materials into one valid `ThemeSpec` that can be pasted directly into Theme Lab.

## Authoritative references

Read these before authoring. When prose and source disagree, the TypeScript
contract is authoritative.

- Theme guide: https://github.com/microsoft/flint-chart/blob/main/docs/theme-spec.md
- Exhaustive ThemeSpec types and allowed values: https://github.com/microsoft/flint-chart/blob/main/packages/flint-js/src/core/theme/types.ts
- Real preset implementations: https://github.com/microsoft/flint-chart/tree/main/packages/flint-js/src/core/theme/presets
- Theme Lab: https://microsoft.github.io/flint-chart/#/theme-lab

Do not invent keys. If a requested decision cannot be represented by
`ThemeSpec`, omit it and briefly identify the unsupported decision outside the
JSON only when the user asked for an explanation.

## Output contract

Unless the user asks for commentary, return exactly one valid JSON object:

- Return the bare `ThemeSpec`, not `{ "theme_spec": ... }` and not a complete
  `ChartAssemblyInput`.
- Do not wrap JSON in a Markdown fence.
- Do not include comments, placeholders, ellipses, or trailing commas.
- Include a stable kebab-case `id` and a human-readable `label`.
- Include only supported fields and only decisions justified by the references.
- Omit unspecified optional fields rather than guessing.

The top-level output schema is:

```json
{
  "extends": "optional-preset-id",
  "id": "theme-id",
  "label": "Theme label",
  "ink": {},
  "type": {},
  "structure": {},
  "marks": {},
  "labels": {},
  "legend": {},
  "dataLabels": {},
  "annotation": {},
  "furniture": [],
  "facets": {},
  "layout": {},
  "chartDefaults": {},
  "compileDefaults": {},
  "interaction": {},
  "variants": []
}
```

Every block except `id` and `label` may be omitted. The skeleton shows the
shape, not a requirement to emit empty blocks.

## Theme boundary

A theme controls presentation and compiler behavior across many charts. It may
decide color, typography, surfaces, grids, axes, mark geometry, labels,
legends, annotations, density, spacing, facets, and reusable chart defaults.

A theme does not choose data fields, encodings, aggregation, filtering,
sorting, chart titles, or data values. Never put those decisions in a
`ThemeSpec`. Outside `chartDefaults`, authored policy must not name a chart
type, positional channel, mark type, field, or backend property.

## Workflow

1. Inspect the supplied references. Extract recurring decisions, not isolated
   decoration from one screenshot.
2. Ask only for missing decisions that materially affect the theme:
   identity, required colors, typography, surface/background, density,
   accessibility constraints, and whether an existing Flint preset is a useful
   base.
3. Separate evidence into system roles:
   - surfaces and text hierarchy;
   - categorical, sequential, diverging, and status color;
   - typography roles;
   - axes, grids, baselines, frames, and structural ink;
   - mark weight, corners, points, separators, and spacing;
   - labels, legends, annotations, facets, and layout behavior.
4. Choose standalone authoring or inheritance.
5. Author the smallest coherent spec that expresses the system.
6. Check every key and enum against `types.ts`.
7. Return the bare JSON object.

## Choosing inheritance

Use `extends` when a built-in preset already supplies the intended compiler
behavior and the new theme is a focused variation. Available preset IDs are:

`nyt`, `economist`, `swiss`, `nature`, `mckinsey`, `datawrapper`, `powerbi`,
`powerbi-light`, `pop`, `cartoon`, `apple`, `de-stijl`, `bbc`, and `material`.

Nested objects merge. Arrays and scalar values replace the preset value. If you
replace `ink.series.categorical`, also consider replacing
`categoricalExtended`; otherwise high-cardinality charts may return to the
base preset's extended palette.

How series colour holds up past the palette and on the page:

- Past `categorical` (and `categoricalExtended`), the largest series keep the
  house inks and the rest take `ink.series.overflow`; with no overflow ink they
  take a grey derived from `ink.text.muted`. A single extra series keeps its own
  name. The renderer's default scheme is never used.
- `ink.series.categoricalText` gives each categorical ink a text variant, used
  where a series is written in its colour (line-end names, matched values).
  Without it, an ink under 3:1 against the plot is darkened in its hue for text.
- `ink.series.minContrast: { fill, stroke }` (defaults 1.25 and 1.6) sets when a
  faint ink is made visible: fills gain a darker edge, lines darken in hue.
- `geometry.point.ink` (`series`, `text`, or a colour) sets the ink of a line's
  vertex dots; by default they take the line's own ink.
- `ink.series.categoricalByCount: { 2: [...], 3: [...] }` states a set for an
  exact series count, when the guide publishes one; `ink.series.repeat: true`
  restarts the palette past its end when the guide says colours repeat.
- `ink.series.byMark: { line, area, bar, arc, point }` (each `{ single,
  categorical }`) gives one family of marks its own inks, when the guide does.
- `ink.series.roles: { other, total, missing }` colours values that play a role
  (Other, Total, No data) in every chart. Do not put particular values (parties,
  products) in the theme: those belong to the chart's field annotation
  `colors`.
- `ink.series.selection.ordered: "ramp"` with `ink.series.ordinal` gives a
  series whose order the chart declares (`sortOrder`) tints of one ramp.
- `geometry.area.fill: "fade"` and `geometry.line.wash: "tint" | "fade"`
  (with `washOpacity`) draw gradient fills; use them only for a guide that
  shows them.
- Mark rules stay with their marks: `geometry.area.edge` is a line on areas
  only; `geometry.band.opacity` and `outlineInk: "series"` are for bars;
  `geometry.band.minLength` keeps a near-zero bar visible;
  `geometry.point.density` (`countable`, `all`, `sparse`) says which lines keep
  dots; `geometry.point.shape` (`circle`, `square`, `diamond`, `triangle`,
  `cross`) is the glyph every dot is drawn as, and `geometry.point.opacity`
  how opaque (unset, a scatter's dots are 0.7; on a full plot shrunk dots rise
  toward solid); `geometry.point.halo: { presence, width }` rings a scatter's
  dots in the plot colour (declare it only where the house's dots carry a ring;
  a halo and an opacity below 1 are not combined, so declare one or the other);
  `geometry.arc.order` (`data`, `largestFirst`), `startAngle` and `hole` state
  pie rules.
- `marks.redundantChannels: ["texture"]` with `marks.texture` draws pattern
  fills on bars, wedges and areas: `pattern: "vary" | "hatch"`, or the guide's
  own order as `patterns` (`solid`, `diagonal`, `antidiagonal`, `horizontal`,
  `vertical`, `cross`, `dots`), lines `ink: "darker" | "white"`. Pair it with
  `redundantEncoding: "always"` only when the guide patterns every chart.

Type roles take the full weight scale (`thin`, `extralight`, `light`,
`regular`, `medium`, `semibold`, `bold`, `extrabold`, `black`, or 100–900) and a
`case` (`upper`, `lower`, `title`, `sentence`, `asIs`) that is applied before
text is measured. State the weight the guide names rather than the nearest
old one. `display` styles a KPI's big number; `annotation` a fitted statistic's
note; `footnote` is not drawn by Flint.

Furniture says where it sits and what it is measured against. `canvasTop` is
the canvas's own top edge (y = 0, outside the margin) — use it for a house that
rules the top of the graphic (the Economist's red line, UNHCR's top bar), with
`frame: "canvas"` to run edge to edge or `"content"` to stay inside the margin.
`aboveTitle` is a line over the headline (a wordmark, a logo); `besideTitle`
sits level with the headline and narrows it; `belowTitle` is a rule over the
plot block. Logos are `kind: "image"` with inline `svg` or a `src`, a size, an
`alt` and an optional `href`. The figure label itself is the chart's
`chart_spec.label`; the theme styles it with `type.kicker`.

Use a standalone theme when the reference system does not honestly inherit a
preset's layout, typography, and presentation behavior.

## Schema map

Use the source contract for exhaustive nested fields and enum values. These are
the authored blocks and their jobs:

| Block | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `ink` | Canvas, plot, panel, text, structural, series, status, and accent colors |
| `type` | Minimum size and role-based typography for headlines, axes, values, annotations, footnotes, and displays |
| `structure` | Semantic categorical/measure axes (and `axis.x`/`axis.y` to style the bottom and left axes by side; `placement` takes `opposite`, `leading`/`trailing`, or a screen side), grids, baseline, and frame. `axis.floating` (`omit`, `keep`, `rangeFrame`) says what the axis lines are where the values do not start at zero: a base that is not drawn there, the window's frame, or a frame spanning only the data (Tufte; Vega-Lite only); leave it unset unless the guide says. Each grid, `grid.zero`, `baseline` and `frame` is a presence or `{ presence, style, dash, weight, color }`; a grid may also take `layer: "front"` (over the marks). `grid.minor: { presence, divisions, on }` draws finer lines between the labelled ones |
| `marks` | Band width, strokes, interpolation, opacity, corners, outlines, points, connectors, intervals, summaries, and separators; `group: { gap, spacing }` (also `geometry.band.group`) for grouped bars — the gap between bars in a group and between groups, each a share of a bar's width or `"Npx"` |
| `labels` | Truncation, flush behavior, and the path category names that do not fit their band take. Leave `overflow` unset for the general path: a row of names `wrap` → `rotate90`; a run of times, dates, years or ranks `wrap` → `skip` (round values only) → `rotate90`. Set `overflow` only where the guide asks for something else, e.g. `["wrap", "rotate45", "rotate90"]` for 45° labels (steps: `wrap`, `skip`, `rotate45`, `rotate90`). Trimming is an add-on to every step, governed by `truncation` (`"never"` forbids it). Flint weighs each step whole and trimmed, at every size down to `type.minSize`, and takes the cheapest within the path's order. `fit` holds the thresholds: `minChars` (4), `turnedLimit` (px or `"40%"` of plot height), `gap` (em), `rowLimit` (px or % of chart width, for names down y). Names that fit are always flat; a row of names is never thinned |
| `legend` | Visibility, ordered placement choices, direction, title, swatches (`swatch`: `auto`, `square`, `circle`, `line`), redundancy suppression, and how several keys stand: `arrangement` (`row`/`stack`), `titlePosition` (`above`/`inline`) and `align` (`start`/`center`/`end`/`spread`), preferences the layout keeps unless the keys would overflow |
| `dataLabels` | Visibility, placement, and ink behavior for values on marks; `anchor` (`end`/`start`/`middle`) for labels inside bars, `fallback` (`perMark`/`allOutside`) when some bars are too short, `minContrast` for the ink inside a bar |
| `annotation` | Units, axis titles, number formatting, point emphasis, labels, and statistics. `numberFormat.compact` sets number compaction: `style` (k/M/B, K/M/B, k/m/b, k/m/bn), `per` (`scale`: one unit per axis, or `value`), `threshold`, `on` (`axis`, `labels`) and the semantic `types` it covers; values already in a scale (`m`, `bn`, "(millions)") are never compacted |
| `source` | How a chart's source line reads, when the chart gives one: `leadIn` (and its weight, style, case), `align`, `frame`, a `rule` above it, a house `credit` (`inline`/`end`/`nextLine`); set in `type.footnote` |
| `furniture` | The header around the title: rules, bands, tabs, wordmarks and logos, placed by `at` (`canvasTop`, `aboveTitle`, `besideTitle`, `belowTitle`) against a `frame` (`canvas`, `content`, `block`) |
| `facets` | Headers, frames, axis repetition, spacing, columns, and scale sharing |
| `layout` | Density, target width, title block, and band step |
| `chartDefaults` | Optional defaults keyed by registered chart type or `*`; caller values still win |
| `compileDefaults` | Preferred base size, canvas size, and supported assemble options |
| `interaction` | Tooltip format and semantic selection-boundary paint |
| `variants` | Conditional policy adaptations; variants may not change `ink` or `type` |

### High-value nested shapes

```json
{
  "ink": {
    "surface": { "source": "house", "canvas": "#ffffff", "plot": "#ffffff", "panel": "#f5f5f5" },
    "text": { "primary": "#111111", "secondary": "#444444", "muted": "#777777", "inverse": "#ffffff" },
    "structure": { "axis": "#222222", "grid": "#dddddd", "frame": "#cccccc", "rule": "#222222", "zero": "#222222", "connector": "#888888" },
    "series": {
      "single": "#0067b8",
      "categorical": ["#0067b8", "#d83b01", "#107c10"],
      "categoricalExtended": ["#0067b8", "#d83b01", "#107c10", "#5c2d91"],
      "overflow": "#777777",
      "sequential": { "stops": ["#e8f3fb", "#0067b8"], "space": "lab", "endpointsAgainstSurface": true },
      "diverging": { "stops": ["#0067b8", "#f5f5f5", "#d83b01"], "neutral": "#f5f5f5", "space": "lab", "endpointsAgainstSurface": true },
      "status": { "positive": "#107c10", "negative": "#d83b01", "neutral": "#777777" }
    },
    "accent": "#0067b8"
  }
}
```

# Flint ThemeSpec authoring

Create a reusable visual system for Flint charts. Translate the user's reference
materials into one valid `ThemeSpec` that can be pasted directly into Theme Lab.

## Authoritative references

Read these before authoring. When prose and source disagree, the TypeScript
contract is authoritative.

- Theme guide: https://github.com/microsoft/flint-chart/blob/main/docs/theme-spec.md
- Exhaustive ThemeSpec types and allowed values: https://github.com/microsoft/flint-chart/blob/main/packages/flint-js/src/core/theme/types.ts
- Real preset implementations: https://github.com/microsoft/flint-chart/tree/main/packages/flint-js/src/core/theme/presets
- Theme Lab: https://microsoft.github.io/flint-chart/#/theme-lab

Do not invent keys. If a requested decision cannot be represented by
`ThemeSpec`, omit it and briefly identify the unsupported decision outside the
JSON only when the user asked for an explanation.

## Output contract

Unless the user asks for commentary, return exactly one valid JSON object:

- Return the bare `ThemeSpec`, not `{ "theme_spec": ... }` and not a complete
  `ChartAssemblyInput`.
- Do not wrap JSON in a Markdown fence.
- Do not include comments, placeholders, ellipses, or trailing commas.
- Include a stable kebab-case `id` and a human-readable `label`.
- Include only supported fields and only decisions justified by the references.
- Omit unspecified optional fields rather than guessing.

The top-level output schema is:

```json
{
  "extends": "optional-preset-id",
  "id": "theme-id",
  "label": "Theme label",
  "ink": {},
  "type": {},
  "structure": {},
  "marks": {},
  "labels": {},
  "legend": {},
  "dataLabels": {},
  "annotation": {},
  "furniture": [],
  "facets": {},
  "layout": {},
  "chartDefaults": {},
  "compileDefaults": {},
  "interaction": {},
  "variants": []
}
```

Every block except `id` and `label` may be omitted. The skeleton shows the
shape, not a requirement to emit empty blocks.

## Theme boundary

A theme controls presentation and compiler behavior across many charts. It may
decide color, typography, surfaces, grids, axes, mark geometry, labels,
legends, annotations, density, spacing, facets, and reusable chart defaults.

A theme does not choose data fields, encodings, aggregation, filtering,
sorting, chart titles, or data values. Never put those decisions in a
`ThemeSpec`. Outside `chartDefaults`, authored policy must not name a chart
type, positional channel, mark type, field, or backend property.

## Workflow

1. Inspect the supplied references. Extract recurring decisions, not isolated
   decoration from one screenshot.
2. Ask only for missing decisions that materially affect the theme:
   identity, required colors, typography, surface/background, density,
   accessibility constraints, and whether an existing Flint preset is a useful
   base.
3. Separate evidence into system roles:
   - surfaces and text hierarchy;
   - categorical, sequential, diverging, and status color;
   - typography roles;
   - axes, grids, baselines, frames, and structural ink;
   - mark weight, corners, points, separators, and spacing;
   - labels, legends, annotations, facets, and layout behavior.
4. Choose standalone authoring or inheritance.
5. Author the smallest coherent spec that expresses the system.
6. Check every key and enum against `types.ts`.
7. Return the bare JSON object.

## Choosing inheritance

Use `extends` when a built-in preset already supplies the intended compiler
behavior and the new theme is a focused variation. Available preset IDs are:

`nyt`, `economist`, `swiss`, `nature`, `mckinsey`, `datawrapper`, `powerbi`,
`powerbi-light`, `pop`, `cartoon`, `apple`, `de-stijl`, `bbc`, and `material`.

Nested objects merge. Arrays and scalar values replace the preset value. If you
replace `ink.series.categorical`, also consider replacing
`categoricalExtended`; otherwise high-cardinality charts may return to the
base preset's extended palette.

How series colour holds up past the palette and on the page:

- Past `categorical` (and `categoricalExtended`), the largest series keep the
  house inks and the rest take `ink.series.overflow`; with no overflow ink they
  take a grey derived from `ink.text.muted`. A single extra series keeps its own
  name. The renderer's default scheme is never used.
- `ink.series.categoricalText` gives each categorical ink a text variant, used
  where a series is written in its colour (line-end names, matched values).
  Without it, an ink under 3:1 against the plot is darkened in its hue for text.
- `ink.series.minContrast: { fill, stroke }` (defaults 1.25 and 1.6) sets when a
  faint ink is made visible: fills gain a darker edge, lines darken in hue.
- `geometry.point.ink` (`series`, `text`, or a colour) sets the ink of a line's
  vertex dots; by default they take the line's own ink.
- `ink.series.categoricalByCount: { 2: [...], 3: [...] }` states a set for an
  exact series count, when the guide publishes one; `ink.series.repeat: true`
  restarts the palette past its end when the guide says colours repeat.
- `ink.series.byMark: { line, area, bar, arc, point }` (each `{ single,
  categorical }`) gives one family of marks its own inks, when the guide does.
- `ink.series.roles: { other, total, missing }` colours values that play a role
  (Other, Total, No data) in every chart. Do not put particular values (parties,
  products) in the theme: those belong to the chart's field annotation
  `colors`.
- `ink.series.selection.ordered: "ramp"` with `ink.series.ordinal` gives a
  series whose order the chart declares (`sortOrder`) tints of one ramp.
- `geometry.area.fill: "fade"` and `geometry.line.wash: "tint" | "fade"`
  (with `washOpacity`) draw gradient fills; use them only for a guide that
  shows them.
- Mark rules stay with their marks: `geometry.area.edge` is a line on areas
  only; `geometry.band.opacity` and `outlineInk: "series"` are for bars;
  `geometry.band.minLength` keeps a near-zero bar visible;
  `geometry.point.density` (`countable`, `all`, `sparse`) says which lines keep
  dots; `geometry.point.shape` (`circle`, `square`, `diamond`, `triangle`,
  `cross`) is the glyph every dot is drawn as, and `geometry.point.opacity`
  how opaque (unset, a scatter's dots are 0.7; on a full plot shrunk dots rise
  toward solid); `geometry.point.halo: { presence, width }` rings a scatter's
  dots in the plot colour (declare it only where the house's dots carry a ring;
  a halo and an opacity below 1 are not combined, so declare one or the other);
  `geometry.arc.order` (`data`, `largestFirst`), `startAngle` and `hole` state
  pie rules.
- `marks.redundantChannels: ["texture"]` with `marks.texture` draws pattern
  fills on bars, wedges and areas: `pattern: "vary" | "hatch"`, or the guide's
  own order as `patterns` (`solid`, `diagonal`, `antidiagonal`, `horizontal`,
  `vertical`, `cross`, `dots`), lines `ink: "darker" | "white"`. Pair it with
  `redundantEncoding: "always"` only when the guide patterns every chart.

`regular`, `medium`, `semibold`, `bold`, `extrabold`, `black`, or 100–900) and a
`case` (`upper`, `lower`, `title`, `sentence`, `asIs`) that is applied before
text is measured. State the weight the guide names rather than the nearest
old one. `display` styles a KPI's big number; `annotation` a fitted statistic's
note; `footnote` is not drawn by Flint.

Furniture says where it sits and what it is measured against. `canvasTop` is
the canvas's own top edge (y = 0, outside the margin) — use it for a house that
rules the top of the graphic (the Economist's red line, UNHCR's top bar), with
`frame: "canvas"` to run edge to edge or `"content"` to stay inside the margin.
`aboveTitle` is a line over the headline (a wordmark, a logo); `besideTitle`
sits level with the headline and narrows it; `belowTitle` is a rule over the
plot block. Logos are `kind: "image"` with inline `svg` or a `src`, a size, an
`alt` and an optional `href`. The figure label itself is the chart's
`chart_spec.label`; the theme styles it with `type.kicker`.

Use a standalone theme when the reference system does not honestly inherit a
preset's layout, typography, and presentation behavior.
